newsitem.title: USA: US could keep astronaut off Mir - Clinton adviser.
newsitem.headline: US could keep astronaut off Mir - Clinton adviser.

text.p: Power problems on space station Mir could keep U.S. astronaut Wendy Lawrence from taking a turn on the troubled Russian craft, President Bill Clinton's top science adviser said on Wednesday.

The decision could be made as late as the day before the scheduled Sept. 17 launch of the space shuttle set to take Lawrence to Mir, according to Jack Gibbons, Clinton's assistant for science and technology.

Mir's electricity supply was cut drastically when a space-going garbage scow punctured the station's power-producing module on June 25, and unless that power is restored, Lawrence's flight could be in jeopardy, Gibbons told reporters.
"I think most important in terms of whether the next astronaut, Wendy, goes up, depends more on the power restoration than anything else," Gibbons said.

"If we're lucky, they think they can get maybe 30 to 50 percent of the power back; that would bring then Mir's power level up enough that we would be quite comfortable with continuation," he said. "If they can't get the power up, then that's a real question."
NASA could make the decision not to drop off Lawrence on Mir as late as the day before the shuttle is launched, but a decision now would be premature, Gibbons said.
"There's more highly relevant information to be gained to help that decision in the next week or two," he said.
Russian officials said on Monday that the September shuttle mission to Mir would go ahead as planned, despite a series of accidents at the station that still need repairs.

Lawrence, a 37-year-old commander in the U.S. Navy, is in training at Russia's Star City to go aboard Mir in September for a four-month stay. She is due to replace Michael Foale, 40, a British-born U.S. astrophycist who has been on Mir since May.
Gibbons said a series of mishaps on Mir may have actually enhanced the learning experience of Americans aboard the orbitting Russian ship.

"My guess is, if everything had gone according to the way we hoped it would, we'd come out on the short end of the stick in terms of relevant experience," he said. "Because encountering the unexpected is something that we should think of as inherent in research and also in unforgiving frontiers like the space environment."
Gibbons said the success of the unstaffed Mars rover Sojourner had reinforced the White House space policy's emphasis on robotic space exploration.
"For now, we see no real limitation there in terms of cost-effectiveness of robotics and its spillout into the rest of our economy," he said.

The planned international space station is also valuable, he said, but stressed that science was only one of the station's functions as "one of the largest peace-time high-tech international endeavours that's been undertaken."
"The international space station is not just a science experiment; if it were, it wouldn't be worth it," Gibbons said.
